claims.text: Rapid, controlled cooling by melt spinning will produce an amorphous structure in a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy.
Rapid cooling will improve glass-forming ability relative to slower cooling of the same alloy.
Rapid cooling will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to slower cooling of the same alloy.
The intervention should work when the cooling rate exceeds the alloy's critical threshold for suppressing crystalline nucleation.
Excessively rapid cooling may induce compositional inhomogeneity or phase separation.
Suppressing crystal nucleation and growth produces a uniformly disordered amorphous structure.
Rapid cooling reduces atomic diffusion and mobility during solidification.
Reduced atomic diffusion and mobility allow solidification to bypass the time scales required for crystallization.
Bypassing crystallization produces a homogeneous amorphous state.
The resulting homogeneous amorphous state has greater resistance to thermally induced crystallization.
The rapidly cooled sample will have a larger amorphous volume fraction than the slowly cooled baseline.
The rapidly cooled sample will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the slowly cooled baseline.
Conventional slower cooling typically leads to partial crystallization or a less thermally stable amorphous structure.
Compositions for which reduced atomic mobility is insufficient to inhibit crystal growth may not benefit from rapid cooling.
Cooling rates below the required threshold may not improve glass formation or amorphous-state stability.
